Hosea likewise speaks of all their evils remembered and their schemes coming before the Lord's face. Amos's oath by Jacob's arrogance is preserved without changing its stated object.

relationship: same-book recurrence of earth's disturbance and Egypt's river
rationale: Both passages join the disturbed or shaken earth with its inhabitants mourning and a consummation rising like a river and descending like Egypt's river. Amos 9 explicitly introduces the Lord touching the earth within this repeated description.

relationship: sunset during the middle of the day as judgment imagery
rationale: Amos announces the sun setting at midday and daylight growing dark upon the earth. Jeremiah likewise describes the sun of the woman who bore seven setting while the day is still at its middle, beside shame and threatened sword deaths. Both use the unexpected midday sunset in a judgment setting.

relationship: sackcloth and mourning for a beloved one
rationale: Amos joins sackcloth with lamentation and mourning for a beloved one. Jeremiah likewise tells the daughter of the people to wear sackcloth and make a pitiful lament for a beloved one because misery is coming.

relationship: shared public mourning signs of sackcloth and baldness
rationale: Amos announces sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head. Ezekiel likewise describes people girding on sackcloth, shame upon every face and baldness upon every head. Both extend these mourning signs across the judged population.

relationship: bread and the Lord's word distinguished as human necessities
rationale: Amos announces a famine for hearing the Lord's word rather than for bread or water. Deuteronomy recounts hunger and manna to explain that a person lives by every word from God's mouth and not by bread alone. Both distinguish dependence on God's word from physical bread.

relationship: seeking divine communication without receiving an answer
rationale: Amos describes people running about seeking the Lord's word but not finding it. Samuel's account describes Saul inquiring through the Lord while receiving no answer through dreams, clear signs or prophets. Both describe an unsuccessful search for divine communication, in different settings.

relationship: young people pictured with thirst in calamity
rationale: Amos foretells young women and men fainting from thirst. Lamentations portrays a nursing child's tongue clinging to its throat with thirst, alongside infants asking for bread. Both use images of bodily thirst among the young, while the age groups and exact effects differ.

relationship: the condemned cult of Dan and its golden heifer
rationale: Amos condemns people who declare that Dan's god lives. Kings records one of the two golden heifers being placed in Dan and calls the resulting practice a sin. The connection concerns Dan's cult; Amos's separate wording about Samaria's propitiation and Beersheba remains unchanged.

relationship: same-book warning that attempted escape cannot save
rationale: Amos 9 says no fleeing person will escape and no one seeking safety will be saved. Chapter 2 likewise denies safety to the runner, fighter, archer and horseman. The later vision renews the warning that attempted escape will fail; chapter 2 explicitly names military ability.

relationship: heaven and Hades cannot place a person beyond God's reach
rationale: Amos names Hades and heaven as extremes from which the Lord will still retrieve fugitives. The psalm likewise asks where one can flee God's presence, then names heaven and Hades and describes His hand's reach. Amos applies the shared spatial contrast to judgment.

relationship: hidden places cannot conceal people from the Lord
rationale: Amos describes the Lord searching out people hidden on Carmel and reaching those in the sea's depths. Jeremiah likewise asks whether a person hiding in hidden places can remain unseen by the God who fills heaven and earth.

relationship: parallel expression of divine attention for evils rather than good
rationale: Amos announces eyes fixed upon the people for evils and not for good things. Jeremiah uses the corresponding expression of the Lord's face fixed upon the city for evils and not for good things. The connection is that stated direction of judgment, while the surrounding accounts treat captivity differently.

relationship: same-book recurrence of earth's disturbance and Egypt's river
rationale: Both passages join disturbance of the earth with its inhabitants mourning and a consummation rising like a river and descending like Egypt's river. Amos 9 explicitly introduces the Lord's touch as the earth is shaken.

relationship: same-book repeated description of the Lord's power over waters
rationale: Both passages describe the Lord calling for the sea's water and pouring it upon the earth's surface, followed by the declaration that the Lord God Almighty is His name.

relationship: explicit recollection of Israel's departure from Egypt
rationale: Amos includes bringing Israel up from Egypt among the Lord's recalled acts. Exodus identifies the Lord as the One who brought the people out of Egypt and the house of bondage.

relationship: parallel recollection of migration from Cappadocia
rationale: Amos recalls the foreigners being brought from Cappadocia. Deuteronomy describes Cappadocians coming from Cappadocia and settling in the place of the Hivites as far as Gaza. The connection is the stated movement from Cappadocia, without substituting another geographical name.

relationship: announced devastation qualified by preservation from a complete end
rationale: Amos announces removal of the kingdom of sinners but explicitly limits it by saying Jacob's house will not be completely removed. Jeremiah likewise announces an invading nation's destruction of produce and fortified cities, then promises not to bring the people to a complete end.

relationship: winnowing and sifting applied to people
rationale: Amos pictures Israel's house among the nations as being winnowed in a basket. Luke describes Satan's demand to sift Simon and those addressed with him like wheat. Both apply agricultural separation imagery to people, with different agents and settings.

relationship: judgment against sinful people who deny approaching calamity
rationale: Amos condemns sinners who insist that evils will not come upon them. Micah likewise presents corrupt leaders claiming that calamities will not come, then announces Zion's devastation because of them.

relationship: explicit later use of David's fallen-tent promise
rationale: Amos promises to raise and rebuild David's fallen tent and demolished parts. Acts introduces a prophetic quotation about rebuilding David's fallen tent and ruins, directly corresponding to that promise.

relationship: explicit later use of the nations-seeking promise
rationale: Amos speaks of remaining human beings and nations over whom God's name is called seeking. Acts' prophetic quotation likewise names the rest of humanity seeking the Lord and nations upon whom His name has been called. Amos's remaining-human-beings wording is preserved.

relationship: shared promise of mountains dripping sweetness
rationale: Amos pictures renewed agricultural abundance with mountains dripping sweetness. Joel uses the same mountains-dripping-sweetness image alongside hills flowing with milk and abundant water.

relationship: parallel restoration of cities and cultivated land
rationale: Amos promises ruined cities rebuilt and inhabited, with vineyards and gardens yielding food and drink. Ezekiel likewise promises inhabited rebuilt cities and cultivated devastated land, comparing it with a garden of delight.

relationship: lasting settlement pictured as the Lord planting His people
rationale: Amos promises that the Lord will plant the people in their given land without future uprooting. Jeremiah announces an eternal covenant and promises to plant the people in the land in faithfulness, likewise depicting their settlement as the Lord's planting.
